clinicalPearls: Rhodococcus equi is a soil-dwelling, partially acid-fast Gram-positive coccobacillus associated with horses and other livestock and their manure

It is a facultative intracellular pathogen that survives within macrophages, so disease occurs predominantly in patients with impaired cell-mediated immunity, classically advanced HIV and transplant recipients
The hallmark presentation is a subacute, granulomatous, cavitating pneumonia that develops over weeks with fever, cough, and weight loss
Chest imaging often shows upper-lobe consolidation with cavitation and sometimes an air-fluid level, and blood cultures are frequently positive in immunocompromised hosts
Extrapulmonary spread can produce brain abscess, osteomyelitis, lymphadenitis, and bacteraemia
The organism may be dismissed as a diphtheroid contaminant in the laboratory, so a compatible clinical picture should prompt careful identification, aided by its salmon-pink colonies
Treatment requires prolonged combination therapy, typically a macrolide-based regimen paired with agents such as rifampicin or a fluoroquinolone, together with restoration of immune function
reference.pathophysiology: Rhodococcus equi is an environmental actinomycete found in soil enriched by the manure of horses and other herbivores. Humans are usually infected by inhalation of contaminated dust, and less often through wound inoculation or ingestion. As a facultative intracellular organism it is taken up by alveolar macrophages, where a virulence plasmid encoding virulence-associated proteins allows it to survive and replicate within the phagosome, subverting normal killing. Effective containment depends on T-cell-mediated macrophage activation, which explains why serious disease is concentrated in patients with defective cellular immunity. Uncontrolled intracellular growth drives a granulomatous, necrotising, and often cavitating pneumonia; sometimes the histology shows malakoplakia with characteristic intracytoplasmic inclusions. Haematogenous dissemination can seed the brain, bone, and other sites.
additionalDifferentials: Pulmonary tuberculosis and non-tuberculous mycobacterial disease
Invasive pulmonary aspergillosis or other fungal cavitary disease
Pneumocystis or other opportunistic pneumonia in HIV
additionalInvestigations: Sputum, blood, and respiratory-sample cultures with careful identification of the coccobacillus (salmon-pink colonies, partial acid-fastness)
Chest radiography and CT to characterise cavitary upper-lobe disease
HIV testing with CD4 count and assessment of other immunosuppression
Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage or biopsy where sputum is unrevealing
Antimicrobial susceptibility testing to guide combination therapy
Imaging of the brain and other sites if dissemination is suspected
redFlags: Cavitating pneumonia with bacteraemia in an immunocompromised patient
Neurological signs suggesting brain abscess from dissemination
Rapid clinical deterioration or respiratory failure
Relapse or persistent infection despite therapy indicating inadequate immune reconstitution
reference.prognosis: Outcome hinges on immune status and prompt, prolonged combination therapy; with restoration of cell-mediated immunity (for example effective antiretroviral therapy) many patients recover, but disseminated disease in profoundly immunosuppressed hosts carries appreciable mortality and a risk of relapse.
pitfalls: Dismissing the isolate as a diphtheroid skin contaminant and missing a true pathogen
Using single-agent or short-course therapy, which promotes relapse and resistance
Overlooking the animal or soil exposure history in an immunocompromised patient with cavitary pneumonia
Failing to address the underlying immunosuppression, without which cure is difficult
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
management: Prolonged combination antimicrobial therapy with intracellular-active agents such as macrolides, rifampicin, fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides and, in severe disease, carbapenems or vancomycin, avoiding beta-lactam monotherapy because of relapse
Restore cell-mediated immunity by starting antiretroviral therapy in HIV and reducing immunosuppression in transplant recipients
Susceptibility testing to tailor the combination and guard against emergent resistance
Drainage or surgical resection of persistent abscesses or cavitary necrotic lung disease that fails to respond
Imaging and directed treatment of extrapulmonary foci such as brain abscess and osteomyelitis when dissemination is suspected
Prolonged clinical and radiological follow-up to detect relapse after stopping therapy
Coordinated infectious-diseases, HIV and transplant specialist input
